summary: Defines Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers, which shorten the gap when a mobile node moves from one access router to another. During that gap the node cannot send or receive packets because of link-switching delay and IP protocol operations.

plainLanguage.summary: Fast handovers let a Mobile IPv6 device prepare for a new network before it disconnects from the old one. The previous router can forward packets during the move, but the protocol does not shorten the link-switching delay.

subtitle: Mobile IPv6 fast handovers prepare a new router and address before a device changes links.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 device may lose connectivity while it detects a move, configures an address, and updates bindings with other nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The device learns about a neighboring router and forms a prospective address before moving. Its previous router can then forward packets to the new address while the device attaches.
tldr.outcome: The protocol reduces latency from IP-layer operations, not link switching. RFC 5568 obsoletes RFC 5268 and is updated by RFC 7411.

today: RFC 5568 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5268 and is updated by RFC 7411.

sections.title: Reducing the IP-Layer Handover Gap
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile node keep connectivity while changing access routers. Normal movement detection, address setup, and binding updates can leave a period when packets cannot be sent or received.

RFC 5568 defines IP messages to reduce this protocol-related delay. It does not improve the time needed to switch the underlying link or change the node's normal Mobile IPv6 signaling with its home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: A move between access routers can interrupt packet delivery while the device updates its IP information. This protocol prepares some of that information before the move, but does not speed up the link change.

sections.title: The Mobile Node and Its Routers
sections.content:
The Mobile Node (MN) moves between a Previous Access Router (PAR) and a New Access Router (NAR). Its Previous Care-of Address (PCoA) is valid on the PAR subnet; its New Care-of Address (NCoA) is intended for the NAR subnet.

In predictive operation, the MN sends its Fast Binding Update while still attached to the PAR. In reactive operation, it sends the update only after attaching to the NAR. The NAR can also assign the new address.
sections.plainLanguage: The PAR is the router the device is leaving, and the NAR is the router it expects to use next. Predictive operation sends the update before the move; reactive operation sends it after arrival.

sections.title: Preparing and Forwarding Packets
sections.content:
The MN asks the PAR for information about nearby access points using RtSolPr. The PAR responds with PrRtAdv messages containing router addresses and prefixes, so the MN can form a prospective NCoA before leaving.

The MN sends an authenticated Fast Binding Update to ask the PAR to forward packets for the PCoA to the NCoA. When the MN attaches to the NAR, it sends an Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement (UNA), allowing the NAR to forward arriving or buffered packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The device learns the next router's address information before moving. It asks the old router to forward packets and announces its arrival to the new router.

sections.title: Checking the New Address
sections.content:
The PAR can send a Handover Initiate (HI) to the NAR before setting up forwarding. The NAR checks whether the proposed address is acceptable and replies with a Handover Acknowledge (HAck); it may assign another address.

If the NAR assigns an address, it is returned through the PAR to the MN, which must use it. After attaching, the MN sends UNA and, if no Fast Binding Acknowledgment arrived, sends its update again.
sections.plainLanguage: The old and new routers check whether the proposed address can be used. If the new router assigns a different address, the mobile node must use that address.

sections.title: Buffering, Address Checks and Fast Movement
sections.content:
Packets may arrive before the MN attaches or before the PAR processes its update. Routers may buffer packets, but the RFC requires a default method that meters delivery according to packet arrival rates; up to 5 packets may be sent in a burst.

Duplicate Address Detection can add delay, so the protocol is intended for settings where address collisions are extremely unlikely or not a concern. Rapid or mistaken movement can still lose packets, and temporary tunnels should have short lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers may hold packets until the device arrives, then pace delivery to avoid another burst of loss. Address checks and very rapid moves can still add delay or cause packet loss.

sections.title: Messages and Authentication Data
sections.content:
RtSolPr and PrRtAdv use ICMPv6 Type 154 with different subtype values. Fast Binding Update and Fast Binding Acknowledgment use Mobility Header types 8 and 9; HI and HAck also use Mobility Headers in this RFC.

The FBU and FBack must include a BADF option based on a shared handover key. The default message authentication code uses HMAC_SHA1 with the first 96 bits; other algorithms may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Different message types carry neighbor information, address updates, and router coordination. The binding update and acknowledgment include authentication data so the routers can check them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An unauthenticated FBU could redirect another device's packets. The PAR must verify that the sender legitimately owns the PCoA, and the FBU and FBack use the BADF authenticator based on a security association.

The PAR must also check that the NCoA belongs to the NAR's prefix. HI and HAck between routers require security associations that provide integrity and data-origin authentication; the RFC requires IPsec support.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication prevents an outsider from requesting that another device's packets be redirected. The routers also check that the new address belongs on the new router's subnet.

messages.label: FBU
messages.note: Requests forwarding to the new address.
